Thanks again for taking the demo this morning — appreciate the clear framing of the primary questions: how do you want us to think about unit pricing (tokens vs characters vs requests), how prompt caching affects billing, and what a reasonable $/1M-token target looks like against your budget. Quick recap and next steps from our side: 

Key takeaways from the demo
- You expect ~1.2k–2.5k end-user interactions/day initially (chat-style usage).
- Typical prompt sizes looked like 80–200 tokens; average completion ~60–150 tokens (varies by use-case).
- Main confusion: how tokens relate to characters and whether cached responses still get billed as tokens.

What I’m sending you today
- A short explainer with worked examples (attached: redwood-pricing-quick-math.xlsx).
- A sketch of cache behavior and where savings come from (attached PNG).
- A one-page estimate for three usage scenarios (low / medium / high). Link to the working HubSpot deal and shared Drive in case you want to edit numbers: https://app.hubspot.com/contacts/1234567/deal/FTX-4389

Short answers up front
- Billing unit: we use tokens as the canonical billing unit (not characters).
- Characters: useful for rough estimation (avg ~4 characters per token in English) but not used for billing.
- Requests: counted for rate limiting / request quotas but not the same as tokens — you can have many small requests or fewer larger ones.
- Caching: prefix/KV caching reduces model computation and therefore lowers billed tokens in practice; full cache hits (identical prompt + parameters) serve from cache and do not incur model compute charges.

Next steps
1) I’ll attach worked examples — please drop in a sample transcript if you want tighter estimates.
2) Karthik / Marissa will check discount/contract mechanics once you confirm scenario.
3) If helpful, we can run a short instrumented pilot to measure real token counts against your actual traffic.

2) For caching: if an identical prompt has been seen before and you return a cached response, do we still get billed for those tokens? We have a lot of repeated-tool prompts that we hope to avoid paying for repeatedly.

Sara — great questions. Below are short, explicit answers plus a worked example using the numbers you gave (1500 chars ~ 350 tokens prompt + 120 tokens completion). I also include a recommendation for how to think about a target $/1M tokens for your expected workload.

Definitions (short)
- Token: the billing unit. We bill based on tokens processed by the model during inference. That includes prompt tokens (the context we feed into the model) AND completion tokens (what the model generates).
- Character: not a billing unit. Useful for estimating tokens quickly: in English, a rule of thumb is ~3.5–4.5 characters per token (we use ~4 chars/token for quick math).
- Request: an API call. Requests are tracked for throttling/quotas; some contracts include a per-request fee but token billing is the primary metering mechanism.

Caching behavior (how it affects billing)
- Full cache hit (identical prompt + model + params): we serve the cached payload and you are NOT billed for model compute tokens. There is no token compute charge on cache hits.
- Prefix / KV cache: this avoids reprocessing earlier tokens on the model side and reduces the number of prompt tokens that need to be recomputed. You still pay for tokens returned to the client (completion tokens) but prompt-side work can be reduced, lowering billed tokens when the model doesn’t need to process repeated prefixes.
- Practical: caching reduces billed tokens when it prevents the model from doing work. If you have many identical prompts (FAQ-like queries), caching can dramatically lower billed tokens.

Worked example using your numbers
- Your numbers: prompt ~350 tokens; completion ~120 tokens => per interaction = 470 tokens.
- Conversion: 1 token ≈ 4 chars => 470 tokens ≈ 1,880 characters (aligns with your 1,500-char estimate given tokenizer variance).

Cost math (example price for illustration)
- If price = $6.00 per 1,000,000 tokens: 1M tokens = $6.00.
- Cost per interaction = 470 / 1,000,000 * $6.00 = $0.00282 per interaction.
- If you do 2,000 interactions/day => 940,000 tokens/day => ~0.94M tokens/day => daily cost ≈ $5.64; monthly (30 days) ≈ $169.20.

How to think about $/1M token target
- $/1M tokens is the clean way to compare unit economics across vendors. For your use case (interactive chat with ~470 tokens/interaction), the levers are: reduce completion length (smaller generated outputs), use prefix/KV caching for repeated prefixes, and batch background tasks.
- If your procurement target is to keep the monthly bill under $X (you mentioned $2k/month as a rough procurement threshold), we can back into a $/1M target given your projected usage. With 2k interactions/day and 470 tokens/interaction (~28.2M tokens/month), to hit $2k/month your effective price must be <= $2,000 / 28.2 ≈ $70.9 per 1M tokens. (Note: that is a procurement target and includes other line items we can discuss — compute vs storage/observability fees.)

Other notes
- Tokenizers differ by model: exact token counts will vary slightly depending on model family. We include tokenizer-preview tooling as part of onboarding so you can run a few transcripts and see exact counts.
- Requests vs tokens: if you have many tiny requests (e.g., 20 tokens each), request-rate limits and per-request overhead matter even if token cost is low. We can discuss a blended plan if you have extreme QPS.

I updated the spreadsheet with the worked example and a short sheet that shows how caching changes the monthly token total for a repeated-prompt scenario. See attached. If this looks right, we’ll:
1) mark which scenario you prefer,
2) have Karthik/Marissa propose contract terms (including any volume discounts),
3) optionally run a 2-week pilot that measures real token counts.

Happy to hop on 30 mins if you want to walk the numbers together.

Best,
Diego
